title: P-L-L
hookLine: tefillah; the verb for praying is reflexive, and many read it as judging oneself

cards: A woman is standing in the sanctuary at Shiloh. Her name is Hannah, and she has no children. Her lips are moving, but there's no sound.
The book of Samuel says: "only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard." The priest Eli watches her, decides she's drunk, and tells her to put away her wine. She isn't drunk.
She's pouring out her heart. The text says she "prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." Silent, inward, completely honest.
What she was doing has a Hebrew word, and its three letters are today's root.

teach.b: P-L-L. Pe, lamed, lamed. From it comes tefillah, prayer.
Turn it four ways. First, the courtroom. In Exodus, a fine is set, and a man "shall pay as the judges determine."
Judges there is from this root: judging, weighing, deciding. Second, one verse that holds both.
Eli warns his sons: "If one man sin against another, the judge shall judge him: but if a man sin against the LORD, who shall intreat for him?"
Judge, and intreat, which means plead or pray: the same letters, a few words apart. Third, the verb.

teach.h: A VERB TURNED BACK ON ONESELF.
teach.b: To pray is l'hitpallel, built in a form Hebrew often uses for actions turned back on oneself, like getting dressed or washing up.
Some teachers read it this way: to pray is to judge yourself, to stand in front of the truth about your own life. Others hear it as standing before the Judge, or as pleading.
These readings sit side by side, and they don't cancel each other out. Fourth, Hannah.
The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, draws lessons about prayer from her: say the words in the heart, let the lips move, keep the voice low.
Her prayer wasn't a performance for Eli or anyone. It was a long, honest look inward, said to God. So the root gives prayer a mirror as well as a window.

how: Jews say the Amidah, the standing prayer of the daily services, quietly, with the lips moving and the voice low, a practice the Talmud draws from Hannah's prayer.

games.q: you're Hannah. you've just poured out your heart in silence, and the priest accuses you of being drunk. what do you do?
o: tell him plainly you're not drunk; you've been pouring out your soul.
start praying out loud so he can hear.
games.why: Hannah answers Eli that she has drunk nothing and has poured out her soul before the LORD; he blesses her and sends her in peace.

practice: Let your face go still and ask one plain question about the last day: where was I at my best, and where did I fall short? Don't argue with the answer or dress it up; look the way a fair judge looks, clearly and without cruelty.
If you pray, you can bring what you saw into your prayer, lips moving and voice low, the way Hannah did; if you don't, simply stay with what's true for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: P-L-L. Pe, lamed, lamed: to judge, to plead, and in its turned-back form, to pray. The root of tefillah. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: prayer; from the root pe, lamed, lamed, which also carries judging and pleading.
